title: Building Meaning Atlas, the struggles, changes and learning behind the website

body:
When I started building Meaning Atlas, I already had an idea of what I wanted it to become, a way of showing how words can carry different meanings depending on who is using them, where they come from and what someone is trying to express. But having the idea and actually making it work as a website were two different things. I had to think about how people would add their words, how the meanings would be shown, and how someone else could look at them without assuming that because two words were connected they meant the same thing.

The website went through quite a few changes while I was working on it. Some of these were planned and others came from finding problems after I thought a part of it was already finished. Looking back at the code, there are different versions of the same idea still visible in the project, and that is partly because I kept changing how I wanted the website to work as I got further into building it.

Starting with the structure and changing how it worked:

The first version was built using React, with files such as AtlasApp.tsx, ContributeForm.tsx, DetailPanel.tsx, ImportView.tsx, MethodView.tsx and WordWeb.tsx. I also had files for the data, layout, database, backups and the starting examples. There was already quite a lot to the structure, including the questions people would answer when adding a word. I wanted more than just the word and its translation, so the form included things like the meaning, an example, how it felt, the context it was used in, the intention behind it and whether it connected to someone's identity. I also wanted people to be able to add images, audio or video to help explain something that writing alone might not explain properly.

As I kept working on the website, I started changing parts of the structure and how people would move through it. I wanted the words to be visible as part of a larger collection, not just something you read in a list and leave. This was where the map and the shelves started becoming more important. The map could show connections between words through shared labels, while the shelves gave people another way to browse the collection and spend more time looking at individual entries.

Then I had to change the way the website was being served. The React version was not the version I ended up using for the live GitHub Pages site, so I made a separate static version using index.html, css/atlas.css and JavaScript files including js/app.js, js/core.js, js/data.js and later js/site.js. The text used across the site was also moved into js/copy.json. Some of the earlier React and server-related files are still in the repository, but GitHub Pages does not run that version of the application.

This is one of the reasons the code can look a bit inconsistent when someone looks through it. It was not one straight process where I built everything in the same way and then published it. I changed the approach and kept working on the version I could actually use for the project. I had to make sure that the public link opened the atlas directly as well, rather than leaving visitors on a separate landing page that did not really need to be there.

The map, the shelves and what I was trying to show:

A lot of the work was figuring out how the information should look and how someone would understand what they were seeing. The visual design changed from a lighter white and green style to a darker background with lilac and gold. I wanted the words and their connections to stand out, but the map also had to remain readable when more information was added. Some labels started overlapping and the layout became too cramped, especially when I looked at narrower screens. I changed how the map was arranged on smaller screens and worked on the spacing so that it would not simply become a smaller version of the desktop layout.

The shelves had their own problems. Some of the text was difficult to read against the dark background, so I changed the book pages to a lighter paper colour. I also had to adjust the controls because the way something looks and the way it behaves are not always the same thing. At one point, the back control did not behave the way I wanted when someone was looking through a word, so I changed it to close the book properly. These are smaller things, but they affect whether someone can actually use the site without having to stop and figure out what a button is supposed to do.

The connections themselves were something I had to be careful with. I did not want the map to make it look as if two words were connected because they had exactly the same meaning. Instead, the lines appear when two accounts share a label on the selected layer, such as emotion, context or intention. When someone clicks a line, they can see both words and the label that connects them. The website also explains that sharing a label does not mean the words have the same meaning.

That distinction matters to the project because the point is not to turn every word into a direct translation of another one. Someone might describe two expressions using a similar emotion, but the circumstances in which they would use them could be completely different. I wanted the connections to give people a reason to look closer, not make the decision for them.

I also changed the form so that an entry needed an example, an emotion, a context and an intention, as well as at least one label that the person selected themselves for each layer. I had experimented with automatic suggestions, including suggestions around joy and approval, but I removed those because I did not want the site to keep pushing people towards labels that might not fit what they were trying to say. It made more sense for the person contributing the word to decide how they wanted to describe it.

Getting the words to stay there:

One of the more frustrating parts was getting the shared data to work. The website could look fine on my own browser, but that did not mean the same words would appear when someone opened it somewhere else. I initially used CrudCrud to store and retrieve the shared records, but I hit its limit of 100 requests. Using more of the same service was not going to solve the problem, so I moved to a key-value store and had to change how the records were saved.

The records were split into smaller pieces of around 180 characters, with keys such as w-{id}-{n} used to store the different chunks. I also had to keep track of the word IDs, account list, owner text and revision information. It was not just a case of saving a word and loading it again, because I needed the different parts of the site to agree on what data was current. I changed the loading and syncing behaviour so the words would be available before the map was drawn, and removed the earlier approach of repeatedly polling every 12 seconds.

There were other problems that took longer to notice. A guest could get stuck behind a message saying the words were being brought in, so I removed that blockage to let guests go straight to the map. I added the ability for people to delete their own words, but then deleted words started appearing again in the guest view because old data was being saved back. I had to introduce a shared list of deleted IDs and revision checking to deal with that. Even after changing the code, cached files could mean the browser was still using an older version, so I changed the script query strings and sometimes needed a hard refresh to see the changes.

Working through these problems made me realise how different it is to test a feature by itself and to test it as part of the whole website. A button can work, a word can save and the map can display it, but the process can still fail when another browser loads an older version or when data is saved in a different order. I had to keep going back to the actual experience of using the site instead of assuming that because I had fixed the code, the problem was gone.

Accounts were another part of this. I wanted people to be able to contribute without having to put their names on everything, so the site creates a user ID beginning with U- followed by 12 characters. The ID initially works as the passphrase, and people can change that passphrase later. The passphrase is stored as a SHA-256 hash rather than plain text. People can also choose whether to add a name or contact detail, and whether similar words should be shown. A person's name is not automatically shown on every word, since the display choice is made for each entry.

There are still limits to this setup. The shared data can be read by someone who inspects the page's JavaScript, the owner login is checked on the client side rather than through server authentication, and media files are kept in the local browser rather than being synced with the shared records. The earlier server and authentication work remains in the repository, but it is not what the live GitHub Pages version is running. I wanted to get the shared words and the main interaction working, but I also needed to be clear about what the current version does and does not protect.

Looking back at the code and the work:

The repository might look like a lot of different things were put together, and in some ways they were. There are the earlier React files, the static website, the server-related work and the changes made while trying to get everything working. Some parts were rewritten and others stayed in the project even though they were no longer part of the live version. When I was fixing something, I was often working around what was already there while also changing what I wanted the site to do.

I used coding assistance for checking errors and working through fixes, including tools such as Copilot and Grok through my coding workflow. That was part of the process, but the website also went through decisions about what information to collect, what the map should show, how the shelves should work and what people should be allowed to display. The code alone does not explain all of those decisions, and I do not want to describe the project as if every part appeared in one finished version from the beginning.

One thing I noticed was that making the website look right was only one part of getting it to work. I could spend time changing the colours or spacing and then find that a word was not appearing on another browser, or that deleting it did not really remove it from the shared view. Sometimes the fix was quite small, but finding out why the problem was happening took longer. And then there were things I had to reconsider because the way I had first imagined a feature did not work as well once I tried using it.

The current version has a working map, shelves, word contribution forms, account options and shared word data, along with a small starting collection. There are five records at the moment, including the illustrative examples lekker and shame in Afrikaans, as well as survey entries involving Massa in Wolof and Čist račun - duga ljubav, which lists Serbian and Bosnian among the languages used. That is enough to show how the site can hold and connect entries, but it is not enough to make broad claims about the languages or what people generally mean when they use these expressions.

There is still more that could be improved, especially around shared media, the limits of the storage setup and how the website behaves across different browsers. I see this version as a working proof of concept rather than a finished system. The part I am most interested in is being able to put these expressions next to each other and let people explore why they connect, while still leaving room for the meanings that do not fit neatly into a label.

The website and the code changed quite a bit from where I started. Some of that was because I changed my mind, some of it was because something did not work, and some of it was because I only noticed the problem after trying it in a different way. Looking back, that is probably the most useful part of the process for me. I did not just build the features I had planned and leave them there. I had to keep testing what I thought the website was doing against what it actually did, and then decide what needed to change.

Website: https://darkstone007.github.io/meaning-atlas/
